entries.39ef7e1f4e05f136e64ef7551b16188691e5abd5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.4.33" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.4.33" sID="gen97005" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.33">Luke 4:33</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">A man having a spirit of an unclean devil. This</hi> mode of expression, which Luke employs, conveys the idea, that the man was driven by the impulse of the devil. By the permission of God, Satan had seized the faculties of his soul in such a manner, as to drive him not only to speak, but to perform other movements, at his pleasure. And thus, when the <hi type="italic">demoniacs</hi> speak, the devils, who have received permission to tyrannise, speak in them and by them. The title, <hi type="italic">Holy One of God, </hi>was probably taken from a manner of speaking, which was, at that time, in ordinary and general use. The Messiah was so called, because he was to be distinguished and separated from all others, as endued with eminent grace, and as the Head of the whole Church.<div eID="gen97006" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.4.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97005" osisID="Luke.4.33" type="section"/>
entries.f5772a0a351bacf8eeccf4e87b71d0d4ddf6e8af: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.4.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.4.36" sID="gen97009" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.36">Luke 4:36</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And trembling came upon all</hi> This is the result of the miracle. They are compelled to acknowledge that there is in Christ something more than man, and justly trace the glory and power of the miracle to his doctrine. <hi type="italic">What speech is this, </hi>they say, which even the devils themselves are forced to obey?<div eID="gen97010" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.4.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97009" osisID="Luke.4.36" type="section"/>
entries.95ad025efa126d8988e88ef8d33ce3d0b6ce8275: <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.4.39" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Luke.4.39" sID="gen97025" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.39">Luke 4:39</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">He rebuked the fever.</hi> To a person not well acquainted with Scripture this mode of expression may appear harsh; but there were good reasons for employing it. <hi type="italic">Fevers </hi>and other diseases, famine, pestilence, and calamities of every description, are God’s heralds, <note n="347"> <div sID="gen97027" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Les sergens de Dieu</foreign>;” — “God's bailiffs.”<div eID="gen97027" type="x-p"/> </note> by whom he executes his judgments. Now, as he is said to send such messengers by his command and pleasure, so he also restrains and recalls them whenever he pleases. The manner in which he healed them is not mentioned by Matthew and Mark: but Luke says, that it was by <hi type="italic">laying hands on each of them.</hi> Under the Law, this was a sign of reconciliation; and, therefore, it was not improperly, or unseasonably, that Christ <hi type="italic">laid hands </hi>on those whom he freed from the curse of God. It was also a solemn rite of consecration, as will afterwards be more fully explained. But I interpret Christ’s <hi type="italic">laying hands </hi>on the sick, as meaning simply, that he recommended them to the Father, and thus obtained for them grace and deliverance from their diseases.<div eID="gen97026" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Luke.4.39" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97025" osisID="Luke.4.39" type="section"/>

               <ns0:p n="14">14 And Jesus returned in the power of the spirit into <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Act. 10.37.</ns0:note> Galilee, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 4.12. Mark 1.14.</ns0:note> and there went out a fame of him through all the region round about.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And he taught in their synagogues, being glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rified of all.<ns0:note place="bottom">Both <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> make the occasion of our Saviours going into <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> to be his hearing, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> John <ns0:hi>was cast into Prison.</ns0:hi> But certainly <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> speak of a second going into <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> and mean by it <ns0:hi>Galilee of the Gentiles,</ns0:hi> which was in the jurisdiction of <ns0:hi>Philip</ns0:hi> the Brother of <ns0:hi>Herod Antipas,</ns0:hi> else one might admire, why Christ should go into <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> upon hearing that <ns0:hi>Iohn was cast into Prison</ns0:hi>; that had been for him to have thrown himself into <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi>'s Mouth, before that his time of suffering was come; but it should seem that after his Tempta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions, he first went to <ns0:hi>Capernaum,</ns0:hi> where he did not stay many dayes, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.12. and then to <ns0:hi>Nazareth,</ns0:hi> which was his own Country; but others think that all the Evangelists speak of a second going into <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> which I cannot agree if <ns0:hi>Nazareth</ns0:hi> were within that <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> which was called the lower <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> and was within the jurisdiction of <ns0:hi>Herod Antipas,</ns0:hi> who was the <ns0:hi>Tetrarch of Galilee,</ns0:hi> and the Man that had imprisoned <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> and afterwards caused him to be beheaded. <ns0:hi>And he taught in their Synagogues.</ns0:hi> He had the reputation of a <ns0:hi>Prophet,</ns0:hi> which procured him that liberty of speaking in all those places, where the Jews celebrated their publick worship; being <ns0:hi>glorified,</ns0:hi> that is, admired, and honoured <ns0:hi>of all.</ns0:hi>

It was their manner in the <ns0:hi>Synagogues</ns0:hi> for the Minister (an officer appointed to that purpose see <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19.) to bring the Book of the Law or of the Prophets, which was to be read, and to deliver it to him that officiated for that time, who when he had read, re deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered it to the same Officer to be laid up. Ah! but Christ was no more sent to all <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> than <ns0:hi>Elias</ns0:hi> was sent to all the Widows in <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi> He was sent to Preach to them all, but for any special signal favours, he was sent but to some, and those some were such as did not proudly reject and contemn him<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but receive him.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 And all they in the synagogue, when they heard these things, were filled with wrath.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And rose up, and thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Edge.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> brow of the hill whereon their city was built that they might cast him down headlong.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 But he passing throw the mids of them, went his way.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Vnhappy Nazareth</ns0:hi>! where Christ had now lived more than thirty years, they had seen him growing up, <ns0:hi>increasing in Wisdom, and Stature, and in favour both with God and Man, Chap.</ns0:hi> 2.52. they had had the first fruits of his Ministry, and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. they <ns0:hi>bare him witness, and wondred at the gracious Words, which proceeded out of his Mouth,</ns0:hi> they knew his <ns0:hi>education,</ns0:hi> so as they could not think he had this Wisdom, and knowledge, from any advantages of that, but must have it from Heaven; yet when they hear him Preaching, and but touching them for their contempt and rejection of him, and tacitly comparing them with their Fore-fathers in the time of <ns0:hi>Ahab,</ns0:hi> and Preaching the Doctrine of Gods Soveraign, and free Grace, and hinting to them, that the Grace of God should pass to the <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> while they should be rejected, they are not able to bear him. Thus <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 22.21. the Jews heard <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> patiently, till he repeated Gods Commission to him, <ns0:hi>to go unto the Gentiles</ns0:hi>; then they cried, <ns0:hi>away with such a fellow from the Earth, for it is not fit he should live.</ns0:hi> This was according to the old Prophecy, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32.2. (applied to the Jews by the Apostle, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.19.) that because they had moved <ns0:hi>God to jealousie, with that which is not God,</ns0:hi> he would move them <ns0:hi>to jealousie, with them that are not a People,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>provoke them to anger with a foolish Nation.</ns0:hi> This is further matter of observation, That wretched Sinners, who cannot obtain of their Lusts, to be as good and holy as others, yet are ordinarily so proud, as they have no patience to hear that others are better than they, or have or shall have<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> any more special share in Gods favour. Those of <ns0:hi>Nazareth,</ns0:hi> which were in the Synagogue hearing these things, are filled with wrath, <ns0:hi>thrust Christ out of the City,</ns0:hi> as not <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>it to live among them, and go about to kill him, by throwing him down headlong from the brow of the Hill upon which their City was built. <ns0:hi>But he passing through the midst of them went away.</ns0:hi> How he got out of their hands, when they had laid hold of him, the Scripture doth not tells us, nor is it our concern to be curious to inquire; we read much the like passage <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 8.59. when the Jews had taken up Stones to stone him, we know it was an easy thing for him who was God as well as Man, to quit himself of any mortal Enemies, but how he did it, whether by blinding their Eyes, or altering the Nature of his Body, and making it inpercepti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble by them, or by a greater strength, then they (which the Divine Nature could easily supply his Humane Nature with) who is able to determine?</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 4.13.</ns0:note> came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them on the sabbath-days.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And they were astonished at his doctrine: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 7.29.</ns0:note> for his word was with power.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Capernaum</ns0:hi> was a City in the other <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> under the juris<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diction of <ns0:hi>Philip,</ns0:hi> whither <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> mention our Saviours motion, upon the report of the imprisonment of <ns0:hi>Iohn Philip</ns0:hi> is not only by Historians reported of a less bloody temper, then his Brother <ns0:hi>Herod,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Herod</ns0:hi> having taken away his Wife, it is very probable, that there was no good understanding betwixt him and <ns0:hi>Philip.</ns0:hi> So that two things promised our Saviour more quiet in <ns0:hi>Philips</ns0:hi> jurisdiction. 1. The tameness of his temper. 2. The <ns0:hi>Hatred</ns0:hi> betwixt him and <ns0:hi>Herod.</ns0:hi> It appears from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 23. He had been at <ns0:hi>Capernaum</ns0:hi> before, but stayed very little, hasten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to his own Country of <ns0:hi>Nazareth</ns0:hi> in the other <ns0:hi>Galilee,</ns0:hi> from thence he now again removeth, hearing of <ns0:hi>Iohns imprisonment,</ns0:hi> and seeing the baseness of his Countrymen; when he came there, he keeps on his course <ns0:hi>Preaching</ns0:hi> upon the <ns0:hi>Iewish Sabbath,</ns0:hi> not abolished till his Resurrection. It appeareth by <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 33. That he Preached in the <ns0:hi>Synagogue</ns0:hi> here also. It is said, That the People were <ns0:hi>astonished at his Doctrine. Astonishment</ns0:hi> is one thing, <ns0:hi>Believing</ns0:hi> is another. Men may be some ways and to some <ns0:hi>degrees affected,</ns0:hi> at the Word of God, that yet are far enough from <ns0:hi>belie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving,</ns0:hi> as the most of these <ns0:hi>Capernaites</ns0:hi> were, else Christ had never upbraided them, as he did <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11.23. <ns0:hi>for his Word was with Power.</ns0:hi> That this Phrase is to be understood only of those power<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />full, and miraculous operations, by which Christ confirmed the Word which he Preached to be <ns0:hi>from God,</ns0:hi> I cannot yield, it is better interpreted by <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 1.22. <ns0:hi>He taught them as one that had Authority, not as the Scribes,</ns0:hi> and to be understood of the gravity, and spirituality of his Doctrine, his <ns0:hi>Majesty</ns0:hi> and Life in the delivering of it, and the Power of God going along with it for the conviction of Sinners, to all which were added his miracu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lous operations, of which the Evangelist goeth on giving us a more particular account.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="36">36 And they were all amazed, and spake among themselves, saying, What a word <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this? for with authority and power he commandeth the unclean spirits, and they come out.</ns0:p>
